What to do in your first 30 days as a DevOps engineer
recent_posts.summary: Practical career advice for engineers starting their first DevOps role. The core message: spend your first 30 days learning the existing system before proposing changes. Key actions include mapping infrastructure visually, reading incident reports instead of just documentation, shadowing deployments and on-call shifts, and delivering small low-risk wins like improving logging, adding missing alerts, or writing runbooks. Common mistakes to avoid include immediately proposing tool replacements, touching production without guidance, and criticizing past decisions. The underlying principle is that credibility must be earned through understanding before influence can be exercised.

recent_posts.title: Why you should learn cloud and Docker before Kubernetes for DevOps
recent_posts.summary: Most DevOps jobs don't require deep Kubernetes expertise — it's often listed as a buzzword in job descriptions. The recommended learning path is: cloud fundamentals first, then infrastructure as code, then Docker container basics, and only then Kubernetes fundamentals (pods, deployments, services). Deep Kubernetes knowledge (operators, CRDs, cluster architecture) is only needed for specialized roles like Kubernetes administrator or platform engineer. The post ends with a promotion for free orientation calls to help engineers structure their DevOps learning path.

recent_posts.title: How multicloud architecture works and how to deploy across AWS Azure and GCP
recent_posts.summary: Multicloud architecture lets teams use the best services from AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure together, but introduces real complexity around credentials, networking, and infrastructure duplication. Two main patterns exist: running in one primary cloud while calling services from others, and running full application replicas across clouds for fault tolerance. Both patterns require managing separate SDKs, authentication systems, and networking configs per provider. A practical demo shows deploying a Node.js app across AWS, Azure, and GCP simultaneously using Control Plane, a platform that abstracts away cloud-specific APIs, handles cross-cloud identity and credential translation, provides pre-integrated Kubernetes with observability and service mesh, and enables automatic failover between cloud providers. The demo also covers granting the app access to an AWS S3 bucket regardless of which cloud it runs on, using Control Plane's universal identity concept.

recent_posts.title: Why companies struggle to hire DevOps engineers who think in systems
recent_posts.summary: Companies are struggling to find DevOps engineers not because of tool knowledge gaps, but because few engineers can think across systems and bridge multiple domains. The rare skill is understanding the full software lifecycle from commit to production, and being able to communicate across developer, operations, and security teams. This cross-domain translator role is increasingly in demand as every company becomes a software company requiring deployment automation.

recent_posts.title: How a non-tech professional broke into DevOps and became a Golden Kubestronaut in two years
recent_posts.summary: Anna Pedra, a former industrial engineer in medical devices, shares her journey switching careers into DevOps with no prior IT background. She outlines a 'triple proof strategy' for breaking into the field: professional cloud certifications (AWS, Azure), structured bootcamp training with hands-on projects, and a strong GitHub portfolio. Despite initial interview failures, she landed her first DevOps role at Swisscom after intense months of simultaneous studying, certifying, and applying. She left after less than a year to pursue more relevant Kubernetes and cloud work, and within two years exceeded her original senior salary. Key insights include why certifications alone are insufficient, how portfolio projects drive interview success, and why choosing the right first job matters for long-term career trajectory. She also achieved Golden Kubestronaut status, becoming the first in Switzerland and first woman in Spain to do so.

recent_posts.title: Linux commands tutorial using a real-world log investigation scenario
recent_posts.summary: A practical, scenario-driven walkthrough of essential Linux commands for engineers. Using a realistic web application log investigation scenario, it covers ls, find, cat, grep, sort, uniq, xargs, cp, rsync, rm, and mkdir — demonstrating how to chain them with pipes to solve real problems like filtering error logs, deduplicating entries, redirecting output to files, and backing up directory structures recursively.

recent_posts.title: Software developer to DevOps transition roadmap in 6 months
recent_posts.summary: Software developers can transition to DevOps in 6 months by leveraging their existing programming skills. The learning path includes Linux and cloud fundamentals, infrastructure as code (Terraform), CI/CD pipelines, containerization with Docker, and Kubernetes. Developers have advantages in understanding application architecture and APIs, though monitoring and incident response may require extra focus. The complete skill set significantly increases career value beyond traditional software engineering roles.

recent_posts.title: DevOps demand is exploding in 2026 and how to capitalize on it
recent_posts.summary: DevOps skills are experiencing unprecedented demand in 2026 due to five converging factors: accelerating cloud adoption, Kubernetes becoming standard, cybersecurity requirements driving DevSecOps, infrastructure-as-code becoming mandatory, and AI both increasing DevOps value while creating MLOps demand. Companies struggle to fill positions (staying open 3x longer than other IT roles) because DevOps requires a rare combination of development, infrastructure, automation, security, and monitoring skills. The opportunity window mirrors software engineering's golden period from 10 years ago—high demand, low supply—but won't last forever. With structured learning focusing on fundamentals first (Linux, Git, Docker, CI/CD) then building up (cloud, Kubernetes, Terraform, monitoring), you can become job-ready in 6-9 months. Common mistakes include learning tools in isolation, surface-level sandbox practice, underestimating opportunity cost, and not documenting progress publicly.
